newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Some Balkan countries try common sense for once.
newsitem.headline: Some Balkan countries try common sense for once.

text.p: Rare signs of compromise and common sense surfaced in some Balkan states this week to deal with explosive problems but shattered economies will leave the region vulnerable to upheavals for years to come, diplomats said on Wednesday.
They said the problems in Serbia, Bulgaria, Albania and Greece were different, but a common threat was economic collapse triggering violent popular reactions, regardless of who was in power.
In Bulgaria, the ruling ex-communists bowed to a month of mass anti-government protests, surrendering power and agreeing to elections in April, 20 months early.
"It was a refreshing sign of common sense but the economic disaster is still there and will be a formidable challenge to any government," said one diplomat in Sofia.

Tens of thousands of Bulgarians celebrated into the night after a month-long protest fueled by mismanagement of the economy. Inflation is at 50 percent a month and the lev, the national currency, has collapsed.
The news of April elections brought jubilation. Barricades around the country came down and strikes, in every sector, were called off.
The threat of violence was palpable as the Socialists, the country's ex-communists, finally agreed to go to the country after struggling to form a cabinet and cling to power.
At almost the same time in Serbia, strongman leader Slobodan Milosevic made his first concessions after 77 days of opposition rallies, prompting a cautious welcome from foreign and domestic critics.
Blamed by many for fueling ethnic wars which ripped former Yugoslavia apart in 1991, Milosevic said he had requested that parliament reinstate disputed local elections, as demanded by the protesters.
Although also suffering severe economic hardships, the protests in Belgrade have been aimed at forcing Milosevic and other former communists to accept democratic change.
Compromise and common sense were more elusive elsewhere in the Balkans, serving as a reminder the historic "powderkeg" of Europe remains unstable and dangerous.
Diplomats said Albania may now be the most unstable Balkan state after thousands of people suffered heavy financial losses in collapsed get-rich-quick investment schemes.
"So far it's the tip of the iceberg. Other schemes will fail and the government will have to choose between printing money, and hyperinflation, to pay or political unrest," said another diplomat.
In the southern town of Vlore, riot police deployed water cannon and fired blank shots on Wednesday to break up a protest by people demanding refunds.

Right-wing President Sali Berisha, whose Democratic Party retained power in May elections denounced by some observers as fraudulent, has tried to stop protests with a mix of promises of partial refunds and a tough police crackdown.

"Albania had made economic progress but almost none of the political reforms needed to create a stable country. Now the economy is collapsing as well," said Yannis Valinakis, of the Hellenic Foundation for European and Foreign Policy think-tank.

In Greece, where democracy was restored in 1974 after seven years of military rule, the socialist government faced a renewed challenge this week by angry farmers who have tried to block national roads to press their economic demands.
About 5,000 police, many in riot gear, were dispatched to the Thessaly farm region to prevent the farmers from seizing main roads for a second time in three months.
"Each Balkan state is different but the economic problems, with no easy or quick solutions, will keep coming back to undermine whoever is in power," a diplomat said.
